results.summary: I reviewed ADR-127's lowering in compiler/ember_mir/src/lower.rs and followed it into the typeck desugarings it depends on: `?`, the ternary, comprehensions and `any`/`all`, fused loops, compare chains and `with`. I also read drop elaboration in ember_analysis/src/drops.rs, because it decides whether a drop on a path where the value was never made is removed or given a flag. Most of the design holds up. Each loop condition goes through lower_condition, which ends its temporaries every turn. Every loop body goes through lower_block and lower_stmt, so the per-turn leak behind D-503 does not come back anywhere I looked, including compiler-written loops inside ExprKind::Block. The loop marks for break/continue and the truncation in return look consistent. When a pending temporary is dropped on a path that never made it, elaboration removes the drop or guards it with a flag, and a temporary listed twice only drops once. I found no double drop and no leak. I found two ordering defects. The first is high confidence and is in code ADR-127 itself extended: an early exit runs the pending defers of every scope it leaves before dropping anything, while [CTL-8] works block by block, innermost first. The second is medium confidence and older than ADR-127, though ADR-127's exit order inherits it. A temporary is ordered by when its slot is allocated, not when its value is made. So a call's result can be dropped after the argument temporaries it borrows from.
checked_ok: lower_condition (lower.rs 751-761): copies the bool to an unregistered slot before dropping the condition's temporaries, and truncates only the entries the condition added. The early return when nothing needs dropping leaves the loop header unchanged. Hidden bindings from an ExprKind::Block inside the condition, such as compare-chain $chain locals and any()/all() accumulators and iterators, are dropped in the head each turn.

While loop: temps_mark is taken after lower_condition has truncated, so break/continue drop only temporaries made inside the body. The final false test drops its temporaries in the head before the else block, and break skips else. continue goes back to the head, which evaluates and drops the condition again.

ForRange: start/end temporaries stay pending through the loop and are dropped at the end of the statement. break leaves them alone because of temps_mark, and return drops them. limit, test and last are plain bools.

Return (lower.rs 870-887): own = len is taken before the value; emit_statement_temps(own) ends only the return's own temporaries, then emit_exit_drops(0,0) ends the enclosing ones. The list is not shortened, so the normal path still ends them.

`?` (typeck synth_try, line 12807): it becomes a match with a Block arm holding a Return. The scrutinee temporary is pending when that return runs and gets dropped; the Err payload moved into the return value is a projection move that elaboration already handles on the Ok path.

Short-circuit and/or: a temporary made only on the right-hand side is maybe-made at the join. drops.rs starts temporaries as MOVED (StorageLive moves out, Drop moves out), so the unconditional drop gets a flag or is removed. In a while condition the back edge brings MOVED, so there is no stale double drop.

A local is never in both `owned` and `statement_temps`. The for-iterator splice moves entries across, hidden Lets go only into statement_temps, and Destructure bindings only into owned. lower_place registers some temporaries twice; the second drop is removed by elaboration because the first sets the state to MOVED.

lower_evaluation_step: a hidden Let is registered after its initializer's temporaries, so it drops before what it may borrow. Every user statement inside a hidden block sits in a loop body or arm Block, and those still end at their own statement ends. typeck only emits Destructure for user statements, so no hidden Destructure binding ends early with the hidden block.

Comprehensions (synth_gather/gather_for): the element and if-clause statements sit in loop bodies, so they end every turn. An iterable kept with keep_alive and the for_iterator Let both live to the end of the source statement, iterator dropped first. The any/all Break { depth: loops-1 } leaves the hidden accumulator and iterable to the statement end.
Fused loops (FilterMap): the user's body sits in the Some arm of a match statement. A user break/continue drops the scrutinee, whose payload was already moved into the binding.

Ternary (check_ternary): it becomes a Match, so its condition's temporaries live to the end of the statement, which is right because [EXP-4] covers only if/elif/while conditions. Pattern conditions are refused (E1010), so the 'pattern test' exception in [EXP-4] cannot arise.
Match guards are lowered with lower_operand, so their temporaries end with the match statement. [EXP-4] does not list guards, so that is spec-conformant.

with: it becomes Block[Let item = value; body...], so the value lives to the end of the block, matching [EXP-4]. Defers: return/break inside a defer is refused (E2160/loop labels taken), and the marks of loops nested inside a defer body are consistent.

findings.title: An early exit runs the defers of every scope it leaves before dropping the locals and statement temporaries of the inner scopes ([CTL-8] says block by block)
findings.evidence: Return does `self.emit_statement_temps(own); self.emit_defers_from(0); self.emit_exit_drops(0, 0);` and Break/Continue do `self.emit_defers_from(target.defer_mark); self.emit_exit_drops(target.owned_mark, target.temps_mark);`. Every pending defer at every nesting level is emitted first, then all locals and pending temporaries, merged by cleanup_order. The comment at 875-879 states this as intended. [CTL-8] says: "On every exit from a block, its `defer` blocks run first and then its locals are dropped". The rule applies per block, and a return exits the innermost block first. So the correct order is: the inner block's defers, then the inner block's locals; then the temporaries of the enclosing statement, which ends as control leaves it ([EXP-4]); then the outer block's defers and locals, and so on outward. The normal path does this, because lower_block ends each block on its own. The early-exit path does not, so one program shows two destructor orders depending on the path taken. ADR-127 carried this ordering over to the newly dropped statement temporaries ('then the defers, then the rest'). That puts a match scrutinee's or for-bound's temporary after the outer block's defers. Besides wrong output, this can cause a wrong panic: a RefMut guard or MutexGuard held by an inner local or a pending scrutinee is still active when an outer defer touches the same cell or lock.
findings.program:
struct Marker:
    pub n: int
    fn drop(mut self):
        println("drop", self.n)

fn number(m: Marker) -> int:
    return m.n

fn f(early: bool) -> int:
    defer:
        println("defer")
    if true:
        _m = Marker(1)
        if early:
            return 2
    return 0

fn g(v: int) -> int:
    defer:
        println("defer")
    match number(Marker(30)) + v:
        30:
            return 31
        _:
            pass
    return 0

fn main():
    println(f(false))   # drop 1, defer, 0  (correct: inner block ends first)
    println(f(true))    # spec: drop 1, defer, 2   actual: defer, drop 1, 2
    println(g(1))       # drop 30, defer, 0
    println(g(0))       # spec: drop 30, defer, 31  actual: defer, drop 30, 31

The same thing with a guard is a wrong panic, assuming the usual RefCell API: `defer: println(cell.borrow())` in the function block, then inside an `if`, `g = cell.borrow_mut()` followed by `return`. The spec drops g before the defer runs; the generated code runs the defer while g is still alive, so the run-time borrow check panics. The same misorder applies to `break`/`continue` with a defer in the loop body and a local in a nested block.

findings.title: A temporary's drop order follows when its slot was allocated, not when its value was made: a call result drops after the argument temporaries it was built from
findings.lines: 478-494 (temp registers at allocation), 6320-6325 (lower_operand), 6581-6585 (lower_into_temp), 864-869 (Stmt::Expr), 3597-3602 (match scrutinee); compare 7112-7121 (lower_place re-registers)
findings.evidence: `temp()` registers a needs-drop temporary in statement_temps and cleanup_order as soon as its slot is allocated. lower_operand's fallback (`let temp = self.temp(..); ...; self.lower_into(Place::local(temp), expr)`), lower_into_temp, Stmt::Expr's discarded-value temporary and lower_match's scrutinee temporary all allocate before lowering the expression. So the temporaries made while computing the value are registered after the value's own temporary. emit_statement_temps and ADR-127's emit_exit_drops (sorted by cleanup_order, last first) then drop those inner temporaries first and the result last. [EXP-4] says 'in reverse order of creation', and the result is created after its argument temporaries. Only lower_place's fallback calls `statement_temp(temp)` again after lower_into, which moves the result after its inner temporaries. A Marker passed by address goes through that path, so that common case comes out right. A value passed as itself does not, and a view type is passed as itself (passed_by_address is false for is_view). So a view type with a destructor that borrows an earlier temporary of the same statement (shape B7, [DRP-7]) gets its drop placed after that temporary's drop. Most likely the [DRP-7] check then reports E3060 on a valid program. If the check misses it, the destructor reads a String that was already freed. ADR-127 inherits the order, since its 'last first' exit order uses the same registration numbers. Confidence is medium: the lowering order is clear from the code, but I could not run the region check to see which of the two outcomes happens.

results.summary: I read all of progress_reduction.rs (plan, zero_entry, header_test, Terms::bound, apply, verify_one, guard_semantics, clone_semantics, same_body) and its tests. I also read ADR-120, ADR-155, the decoder macro in ember_rt.h, how the C backend emits Cast, BinaryOp, CheckedBinaryOp and SpanLen, how MIR lowers mut arguments, and the driver's pass order. ascii_runs.rs I read only where it touches the fast loop. I found no real defect. Every way the fast loop could run where the checked loop would panic is refused by plan() or caught by the guard. Only one CheckedBinaryOp may sit in the region, and it must be an i64 Add followed by its own Overflow Assert. Its other operand is proved to be between 0 and a bound in every accepted form. With the loop's back edges cut, the body must have no cycles, every latch must come after the single step, and only the header test may leave the loop. So each iteration does at most one add and moves the cursor at least one byte, which makes the number of adds at most length - cursor. The guard computes total + remaining * upper <= INT64_MAX exactly, including negative totals and INT64_MIN, using unsigned u64 maths: a checked multiply, then LIMIT - (u64)acc. The empty-rest edge (remaining == 0) is only reached after the length and cursor checks pass, and the fast loop then does no adds. The guard itself has no effects and cannot panic. The fast copy differs from the original only in the certified Add and its Assert. Three side notes, none a miscompile: ADR-120 still says no mutating pass follows verification, but ADR-155 added ascii_runs after it (the certificate comment does acknowledge this). same_body does not compare stack_buffers, static_safe, contracts or borrows_used_fields; apply() never changes them, so this only makes the verifier less complete. In Terms::bound, a local stays in the active set when the function returns early, which can only cause extra declines.
checked_ok: Accumulator: only one CheckedBinaryOp may exist in the whole region (`let [(check, statement)] = checks.as_slice()`). It must be an i64 Add whose dest is a plain local, followed directly by `Assert{cond: flag, expected:false, Overflow(Add)}`. `acc + acc` is refused because bound() returns None for acc, and a copied carry (`t = acc; acc = t + x`) is refused because local(lhs) != acc.

Term is never negative: bound() accepts only constants in 0..=LIMIT, the cursor (usize), the step's char (<= 0x10FFFF), locals not written in the loop whose type range is nonnegative and <= LIMIT, copies, value-preserving Numeric/Widen casts (the target range must contain [0, maximum]), BitAnd with one bounded operand (x & a lies in [0, a] when a >= 0), and BitOr/BitXor bounded by min(a+b, type hi, LIMIT). Every other rvalue declines. Floats, u64 or usize outside the loop, signed types outside the loop, and bool all decline.

Values carried from the previous iteration decline: a term operand defined in the loop must have exactly one definition, and that definition must dominate the use in the loop body with back edges cut (Terms::bound checks dominates()).

BeforeStep (length - 1) is only claimed at points not dominated by the step. Because the body has no cycles, every latch comes after the step, and only the test exits, such points always run before the step in the same iteration, after the test has established cursor < length. Length is claimed only after the step.

Iterations are at most the remaining bytes: the step is the only writer of the cursor (it receives the only Ref the whole body takes of it, and the region has no projected writes and no other calls). The step is dominated by the header test `cursor < view.len`, which header_test checks through copies and SpanLen. The decoder (EMBER_TEXT_CHAR_NEXT, and the ASCII step added by ADR-155) always advances 1 to 4 bytes.

Exits, nesting, continue: only the test block may have a successor outside the region, Return and Unreachable terminators are refused, cycles inside the body are refused by the topological check, a latch not dominated by the step (a continue before the step) is refused, and a second StrCharNext is refused.

No effects inside the loop: statements may only be numeric Assigns to plain locals, the certified check, Storage markers or Nop. Terminators may only be Goto, SwitchInt, the step, SpanLen(view) or the certified Assert. BeginAccess and Drop are refused, as are direct and indirect calls. Mut arguments are lowered through an explicit Rvalue::Ref, which the body-wide Ref inventory catches.

zero_entry: walking back from each outside predecessor, it requires the last write to the cursor to be the literal `= 0` of type usize. It refuses moves, drops, Storage markers, call or checked-op destinations, projected writes, cycles, the function's entry block and paths that re-enter the region. Remembering only true results is sound, because a cycle returns false.

Guard maths (apply and guard_semantics): it checks length <= LIMIT, then cursor <= native_len. remaining == 0 goes to the fast loop, which runs no adds. Otherwise `upper` is built (BeforeStep only once length >= 1; Sum adds two values each <= LIMIT, so no wrap, then takes a branch-free min), then a checked u64 `remaining*upper` whose overflow goes to the checked loop, then `product <= LIMIT - (u64)acc`, which as a u64 subtraction equals the exact room for every i64 acc. The fixed rows in the tests (INT64_MIN, -1, INT64_MAX - 7, u32::MAX-sized lengths) agree.

C validity: a Numeric cast i64->u64 is emitted as a plain `((uint64_t)x)`. Unsigned subtraction wraps in a defined way. CheckedBinaryOp uses ember_ck_mul_u64, which writes the result and returns the flag and does not panic. The fast `(acc + term)` on int64_t is reached only when the guard proves it cannot overflow. SpanLen(str) and view.1 are the same `.len` field.

Effect order and panics: the guard reads only view.1, the cursor and acc, all checked readable at the header. The fallback is the untouched original loop. clone_semantics and same_body show that only the Add and Assert change in the copy. The flag is never read except by its own Assert (checked across the whole body), and acc is never referenced through a Ref.

Single entry and retargeting: every non-header region block has no predecessor outside the region. Only outside edges into the header are sent to the guard. The clone's exit edge stays put. verify_one rebuilds the original, proves it again, and compares it with a replay of apply() in every profile before for_codegen.

Interaction with ADR-155 ascii_runs on the fast copy: the checked fallback is left alone through `cold`. The ASCII step runs the step block's statements before `cursor += 1` and sets char = byte (< 0x80), so the BeforeStep, Length and char bounds and the at-least-one-byte progress still hold.

results.summary: I reviewed all of C:\Users\ism19\Code\ember\compiler\ember_analysis\src\temporary_owners.rs against ADR-114 and found no defects. To check it, I traced where the pass sits in the pipeline (ember_driver/src/main.rs:3139): after inlining, versioning and mark_uncounted_handles, and before propagate_copies, list_locals and stack_lists. I also read how the C backend treats Copy, Move and Drop (ember_codegen_c/src/lib.rs: retain_lines_for_rvalue, the ArrayPush and owned-argument retains, the Drop emission). The pass is safe if one fact holds: the new owner (the destination temp, or the array) is not released between the copy and the original drop, and the original drop is reached first on every normal path. When that holds, the object's count can reach zero only at the same release events as before, so no drop, deinit time, Weak.upgrade result or foreign release changes. The code proves exactly that fact. On the local path it rejects any redefinition, drop or storage marker of the destination, and the destination must not be moved, referenced, uncounted or conditionally dropped. On the array path it allows only quiet points: no Call, no Assert, no Drop, no access marker, no projected or non-scalar store, no storage marker of a local that needs a drop. Both paths reject Return and any cycle. A chain of local transfers made in the same stage (A to B, B to C) stays sound, because each transfer's proof puts the next owner's drop after the earlier owner's drop. Applying the array stage after the local stage also stays sound for the same reason. I could not build an Ember program that frees an object early, drops it twice, leaks it, or moves its deinit.
checked_ok: Retain and release in the C backend: Copy retains (Use, ClassUpcast, ClassInterfaceUpcast, ArrayPush with a Copy argument, owned call arguments); Move does not; Drop releases unless the local is uncounted. Turning Copy into Move and turning the old drop into Nop removes exactly one matched pair. Move through either upcast compiles as a plain pointer cast (lib.rs:9060, 9076).

Local transfers: the destination must have exactly one definition (the copy itself), be a counted class or interface Temp, and be not referenced, not moved, not uncounted, with no conditional or projected drop. Between the copy and the old drop, the check rejects any destination definition, drop or StorageLive/StorageDead. The only other way to release the destination would be a Move, a ref or ref mut, or a mut parameter, and the move and reference checks exclude those. Calls inside the interval may run, because the destination keeps the object alive whatever the callee does.

Array transfers: quiet() allows only Nop, scalar or CheckedBinaryOp writes to whole locals, StorageLive/StorageDead of locals that need no drop, Goto, SwitchInt and Unreachable. Every Call, Assert, Drop, access marker and projected or non-scalar write is rejected, so nothing can empty or re-point the list, and no panic hook can run, before the old drop. The push receiver is a ref mut temporary (list_locals.rs:86-121), so a pattern like src.items.push(src) is rejected because src is referenced.

Same-stage chains: if both A to B and B to C are applied, A's interval puts B's drop after A's drop, and B's interval keeps C alive up to B's drop, so C covers A's old drop. Running the local stage first and then the array stage, with uses recomputed in between, gives the same guarantee.

Owned callees are never sinks: only a Temp assignment or the ArrayPush builtin qualifies. After inlining, a callee's owned parameter becomes a Temp; its drop at the end of the callee comes before the caller's drop, and a mem.drop or move of it sets moved, so the transfer is refused either way. Borrowed parameters of an inlined callee are marked uncounted and rejected.

Interaction with mark_uncounted_handles: an uncounted local as source or destination is rejected. A local copied into an uncounted handle has two whole copies, or its only sink is that uncounted handle, so it is rejected. The RC-2c owners (a User local or an owned Arg) are never Temps, so this pass never takes their count away.

Freshness and Sync: the origin chain follows only whole Use, ClassUpcast and ClassInterfaceUpcast through single-definition, unreferenced class Temps back to ClassNew of a non-Sync class; cycles and unknown roots resolve to false and are cached correctly. Correctness does not actually depend on freshness; the restriction is extra caution.

Control flow: the definition must dominate the copy (block-tree intervals plus statement order in the same block). An iterative DFS marks a point active on entry and done on exit, and treats returning to an active point as a cycle; that is correct even when a point is pushed more than once. A definition inside a loop, a copy inside a loop, or any back edge between copy and drop is rejected. Paths that end in Unreachable are accepted, and that is sound because they abort.

Panics and early exits: Assert has only its next edge and a failing Assert aborts, so on the local path the object is alive under either form and nothing can be deinited. A Return between definition and copy, or between copy and drop, is rejected.

Possible compiler crashes: none found. move_copy's unreachable! branches match what sink() accepts. The expect calls in Dominators hold because every reachable block has a processed predecessor and parent pointers always point earlier in reverse postorder. Running out of the interval budget only declines transfers.

Later passes: propagate_copies and narrow_widened_reads touch only scalars. list_locals and reserve_pushes do not care whether the pushed value is a Copy or a Move. No later pass reruns drop elaboration.

Strong-count overflow ([RC-1] u32 maximum): the transfer lowers the count by one for a while, so in theory it could remove an overflow panic. Reaching that needs about 4.29 billion live handles, which is not realistic, so I did not treat it as a defect.

results.summary: I went through every TyKind::Param match in compiler/ember_typeck/src/lib.rs, plus the TyKind::Assoc sites. Inside a body, T.Item and Self.Item are hidden TyKind::Param values. They are built by declare_one_projection and project, and their bounds come from assoc_bounds_of, which the D-532 fix closes with parent interfaces. Bare TyKind::Assoc only survives in interface signatures, and those are resolved before any body is checked. So most of the per-type predicates handle T.Item the same way they handle T: implements, float_param, zeroable, default_initialisation, has_display, unformattable_part, totally_ordered, hashes, the operator and compound-assignment checks, and bound method calls. The real gaps are earlier, where a hidden projection parameter gets its bounds or its identity. I found three. (1) An associated type bounded by a generic interface written bare, or with only bindings (`type Scalar: Add[Output = Scalar]`), records the generic interface itself (`std.core.Add`, no type arguments) instead of `Add[Scalar]`. A type parameter's bare bound does become `Add[T]`. As a result, implementations that state the type are refused, and generic bodies using the operator are refused. (2) When a signature names `T.Name`, a fresh hidden parameter is always declared, even when T's bound already binds Name (`T: Add[Output = T]`, `I: Iterator[Item = int]`). In the body, project() follows the binding, so the signature and the body disagree. (3) A `where` clause whose subject is a projection (`where I.Item: Display`) is silently ignored. D-644 only moved single-name clauses into the brackets, and no other pass reads multi-segment subjects. I did not build or run anything. The confidence levels come from tracing the code paths.
checked_ok: How projections are represented: in a generic body, T.Item and Self.Item are hidden TyKind::Param values (declare_one_projection at 33668, lazy creation in project at 33957). TyKind::Assoc only stays in interface signatures, which resolve_assoc / resolve_signature_assoc rewrite. So every Param-only match (has_display 12443, unformattable_part 12507, format_spec_applies 12660, totally_ordered 27560, hashes 43059, has_operator_method 46866, compound_through_interfaces 46921, unary and binary operator dispatch 30949 / 47893-47912, index and index_set through bounds 30473 / 20072, method calls through bounds 37724 / synth_bound_method 38352, associated calls 35173, for-loop over a parameter 28448, unwrap_or_default 21966, ArenaMap equality 43686) also covers T.Item.
generic_bounds (4870): a hidden parameter's bounds come from its own slot, or by name from the base's bounds. float_param, param_bound_named, implements and synth_bound_operator all go through it.

D-532: assoc_bounds_of closes associated-type bounds with their parents (close_bounds), and declare_one_projection / project close a hidden parameter's bounds and bindings, so parent interfaces reach T.Item the same way they reach T.
implements() on a Param (34061): the Float-implied Copy/Clone/Eq/Ord/Default and the bound lookup apply the same way to hidden parameters.

default_initialisation (34160) and zeroable (34184) both take hidden parameters through the Param arm. zeroable reads current_generics[index] without the name check generic_bounds does. I could not build a case where a hidden parameter reaches it with a mismatched slot, so I am not reporting it.

Default-method bodies (check_default_bodies_opaquely 17870): Item becomes project(opaque Self, Item), a hidden parameter, so no bare Assoc reaches the predicates; apply_where_bounds handles `where Item: X` there.
unify_sides treats Assoc as matching anything, and is_generic leaves Assoc out. Both are only reached with interface-declaration types, so I found no wrong results from them.
ember_types send/sync/copy lists Param and Assoc together (both not Copy, not Send), which matches TYP-17 because generic bodies are checked once and recompiled per instance.

findings.title: A bare generic-interface bound on an associated type records the uninstantiated interface (Add) where a type parameter's records Add[T], so valid implementations and generic bodies are refused
findings.program:
interface Shape:
    type Scalar: Add[Output = Scalar]
    fn width(self) -> Scalar

struct Box2:
    w: f64

extend Box2 implements Shape:
    type Scalar = f64
    fn width(self) -> f64:
        return self.w

fn twice[S: Shape](s: S) -> S.Scalar:
    return s.width() + s.width()

fn main():
    println(twice(Box2(w=1.5)))

Expected: accepted, prints 3.0. Actual: E2040 at the extend ("`Box2`'s `Scalar` is `f64`, which does not implement `Add`") and E2040 at `+` in twice. Writing `type Scalar: Add` with no binding fails the same way.

findings.title: T.Name written in a signature is a fresh hidden parameter even when T's bound binds Name, while the body's project() uses the binding, so the two disagree
findings.evidence:
declare_one_projection never looks at `generics[base_index].bindings`. It always pushes a new `GenericParam { name: "T.Output", projection: Some(..), .. }` and records it in projection_params. A signature's `T.Output` resolves through resolve_projection_chain to that opaque hidden parameter (`if let Some(&ty) = self.projection_params.get(..) { return ty; }`).
In the body, the result of an operator or a bound method goes through `resolve_assoc(ret, concrete)` and project(), which checks the base's bindings first:
```
if let Some(param) = self.current_generics.get(index as usize)
    && let Some(&(_, _, value)) = param.bindings.iter().find(..) { return Some(value); }
```
The comment at 38485 confirms the intent: `Self.Real` of a type parameter is "what the bound binds it to (`Add[Output = T]`)". So `a + b` with `T: Add[Output = T]` has type T, and `it.next()` with `I: Iterator[Item = int]` is `Option[int]`. The declared return or parameter type `T.Output` / `I.Item` is a different, opaque Param. coerce has no rule that equates a hidden projection parameter with its base's binding, so the result is E2020. A parameter typed `x: I.Item` also loses everything the binding provides: `x + 1` is E2040, although I.Item is int. The bindings are already set when the signature's projections are declared (declare_generics fills them at 3579-3582, before declare_projections at 7856 and 10464).

findings.title: A where clause on an associated type (where I.Item: Display) is silently dropped: D-644 only folds clauses on a declaration's own parameter
findings.evidence: The grammar is `where_clause := "where" type ":" bound_list`, and parse_where_clause (ember_parser decls.rs 973) parses any type as the subject, so `I.Item` is accepted. desugar_where_clauses only moves a clause into the brackets when `let ([subject], true) = (segments.as_slice(), args.is_empty())` and the name is one of the declaration's own parameters. A two-segment subject stays in `where_clause`. After that, typeck reads where_clause only for interface default methods (where_clauses_hold, apply_where_bounds, both requiring `let [subject] = segments.as_slice()`) and for `Self: Sized`. A projection clause on an ordinary function, method or extend is never applied to the hidden parameter's bounds and never checked at calls. A clause on T is honoured (D-644), but the same clause on T.Item has no effect. Bodies relying on it are refused, and callers are never asked to meet it.

results.summary: I read the field-access machinery (field_accesses, field_boundaries, field_return_accesses, call_result_accesses, virtual_result_accesses), the D-218 receiver-by-address code in typeck and the dyn adapter in codegen, and the ODR-065 retained-handle lowering (lower_borrowed_place, innermost_handle, handle_in_shared_memory in ember_mir/src/lower.rs). The access-word and getter-carry logic is sound for fields reached through a class handle. A class handle is Copy, so a class-typed field has no word; the compiler covers the nested case by borrowing through a retained copy of the innermost stored handle (E3060 if the borrow outlives the statement), and that works for `o.inner.items`. I found one probable hole, in handle_in_shared_memory: a borrow through a shared `ref` (or a `mut` parameter) to a Copy struct that holds a class handle gets neither a field word nor a retained copy. I have not built or run anything, so the finding is unconfirmed. Not examined: closure captures, Box fields and generics.
checked_ok: field_boundaries correctly gives a word per non-Copy class field along a place, including nested class fields (`h.a` then `h.a.child.items`) and Array/Vec/Span index steps; the `covered` case for `mut self` is limited to Deref-of-self prefixes.

A view of an Array/String field reached through a class handle holds that field's word for the loan region (field_accesses, Rvalue::Ref arm), so a clear, push or reassign through an aliasing handle panics under EXC-1/EXC-19.

D-218 getter carry: field_return_accesses only records loans that reach the return, and the caller maps them onto its own arguments. The fixpoint compares the whole map. Virtual calls use the union of reachable bodies only when every access is a field of the static owner, otherwise a whole-receiver read. Interface and dyn receivers get a whole-receiver read, which is conservative.
Codegen dyn adapter: a view-returning Borrow-receiver method on a class passes `&receiver`, matching receiver_by_address in typeck, so the by-address ABI agrees on both sides.

ODR-065 lowering: a view through a class handle stored in a class field or array element (`o.inner.items[..]`, `o.kids[0].items[..]`) goes through a retained temp copy, and keeping the view past the statement is E3060, so the nested-class and array-of-handles paths are refused rather than unsafe.
Reaching a field through a RefCell guard counts as a read, not a write, of the holding field (inside_a_cell).

findings.title: View through a shared ref (or mut param) to a Copy struct holding a class handle gets neither a field word nor a retained handle
findings.evidence: handle_in_shared_memory ends with `hir::ExprKind::Deref(inner) => { let mutable = matches!(.., TyKind::Ref { mutable: true, .. }); return mutable && !matches!(&inner.kind, Local(local) if self.mut_param_locals.contains(local)); }`. So the handle `r.inner` in `r.inner.items[..]` is judged not to be in shared memory when `r` is a shared `ref S` or a `mut` param, and no retained copy is made. The reasoning (comment 7040) is that a shared ref to a stored handle was itself retained when made. That holds for `ref o.inner` (lower.rs 6276 retains when the pointee type is a handle), but not when the pointee is a struct that contains a handle, such as `ref o.s` with `s: S` and `S` holding a class `Inner`. There `place.ty` is the struct, so counted_handle is false and nothing is retained. Field `s` has no access word: `class_field_has_access_word` requires `!is_copy`, and a `@derive(Copy)` struct whose fields are Copy is Copy, with class handles Copy (copy_with 1822, ODR-051). A write to `p.s` is therefore an unchecked instantaneous store (EXC-17). The `items` word on the Inner object is held, but the thing that gets freed is the Inner object itself, released when `p.s` is overwritten, and no word guards that. field_boundaries yields `r.*.inner.items`, so the view holds only that word. The borrow checker cannot link `r`, a loan of `o.s`, to a write through the aliasing local `p`.
findings.program:
@derive(Copy)
struct S:
    inner: Inner

class Inner:
    items: Array[int]

class Outer:
    s: S

fn main():
    o = Outer(S(Inner([1, 2, 3])))
    p = o
    r = ref o.s
    v: Span[int] = r.inner.items[0..]
    p.s = S(Inner([9]))
    println(v[0])

Expected: a compile error or an exclusivity panic. Likely actual: p.s's old S is overwritten, the old Inner's last count drops, Inner and its items buffer are freed, and v[0] reads freed memory. The same shape with `fn f(s: ref S, p: Outer) -> int:` that views `s.inner.items`, then calls `p.s = ...` and reads the view, called as `f(ref o.s, q)` with `q` an alias of `o`, should behave the same. I could not confirm that typeck accepts `r = ref o.s` for a Copy struct holding a handle, so this is from reading only.

results.summary: I read ADR-134/D-460 and D-467 and the code they name: the typeck receiver handling (lib.rs 38185-38347), the generic method path (synth_generic_method_call), pass_receiver_to/receiver_by_address/borrow_argument, MIR lowering of ClassUpcastBorrowed (lower.rs 599-614, 6148-6178, 2365-2375), the codegen _N_up declaration and emission (codegen 5284-5296, 5703-5715, 5801-5815), and borrows.rs call_result_accesses, virtual_result_accesses, field_return_accesses, resolve_ref_temps and the fixpoint. I found no stale-copy or under-locking defect. The _N_up copy is keyed by the cast's destination temporary, set at every cast and declared beside it, even inside a loop scope. While a view lives, the derived local cannot be written, moved or re-pointed (E3021, E2103 including mut-param/mem.swap re-pointing). No pass hoists the cast. Generators refuse borrows across yield. D-467's union covers every non-abstract body at the slot in the owner's ancestors and all its descendants. Fields use a bases-first prefix layout, so an index below the owner's field count names the same field in every override. Anything else falls back to the whole object. I found one real regression in D-460. With upcast_borrow set, the receiver is no longer coerced, and the early return into the generic-method path never applies the upcast. An inherited generic view method on a derived local therefore passes `ref Derived` where `ref Base` is expected, which gives mismatched pointer types in C. A second, lower-confidence finding: D-460 only handles a plain `ExprKind::Local`, so `self.inherited_view()` inside a derived method (self reads as Deref(Local)) probably still hits the old E3060.
checked_ok: _N_up is per cast-destination temp (codegen 5284-5296, 5806-5813), not per derived local: two simultaneous upcast borrows of one local to different bases get separate copies of the right C types

_N_up is declared by local_declaration both at function scope and for loop-scoped locals (5345, 5554), so it always sits beside its temp; folded_refs only folds Rvalue::Ref temps, so the Cast statement is never skipped

Each execution of the cast re-copies the handle; loops and branches re-run the cast, and no pass (check_hoisting, loop_access, loop_version, kernels, copies, strength_reduce) moves the Cast out of a loop

The derived local cannot change while a view from it lives: E3021 for assignment (RC-5 reject test), moves/scope end through the loan; the callee cannot re-point self (E2103 for assignment, mut-param passing, mem.swap/replace/take, reject_repointing_self)
The removed retain is safe: the object is kept alive by the borrowed local itself for the call and the view's life
Generators: a borrow of a local or class field held across yield is E2221/E2229, so no view/EndAccess through a stale stack _N_up crosses a resume
Constructor ClassUpcastBorrowed casts (to a class, not a Ref) fall to the generic cast path; local_declaration only adds _up for Ref-typed temps, consistent with 5806's Ref guard

D-467: slots built from all non-abstract bodies with class_owner+class_virtual_slot, the same field codegen uses to fill vtables; slot indices are inherited prefixes (assign_class_virtual_slots), so ancestor/descendant bodies at the same slot are the same method
D-467: FuncRef::Virtual.owner is the resolved method's class; the union over within(owner,c)||within(c,owner) covers every override the object can dispatch to (all descendants of owner)

D-467: field indices are object-layout, bases first (class_field_at_info), so index < class_field_count(owner) names the same field in every override's self type; a field only a subclass has, a whole-object access, a non-receiver argument or a by-value self all fall back to whole_receiver_access
D-467 fixpoint is monotone (Some(list) grows, or flips to None = whole object), so an override's later-discovered access is not lost

Inherited virtual getter through the D-460 cast: mapped place (*t2).f is not resolved through the Cast, but it names the same object's access word at run time and result_access_regions falls back to the result's view regions, so the field is held for the view's life
Copy-typed fields (incl. class handles) and @sync classes have no access word (class_field_has_access_word); this is pre-existing EXC-19 design, not changed by D-467

findings.title: D-460 skips the receiver upcast for an inherited generic method: `ref Derived` is passed where `ref Base` is expected
findings.evidence: Before D-460, every inherited borrowed receiver was coerced in the else branch (`receiver = self.coerce(receiver, receiver_ty)`) before the generic dispatch at 38223. Now, when `inherited && receiver_mode == Mode::Borrow && derived && matches!(receiver.kind, ExprKind::Local(_)) && self.receiver_by_address(receiver_ty, def)`, `upcast_borrow = Some(receiver_ty)` is set and the coerce is skipped. The upcast is applied only later, at 38317 (`else if let Some(base) = upcast_borrow { ... ExprKind::Cast { .. to: ref Base } }`). That code is unreachable for a method with its own type parameters, because `if !self.signatures[def.0 as usize].generics.is_empty() { return self.synth_generic_method_call(def, name.name, Some((receiver, receiver_mode, recv_span)), ...) }` returns first. synth_generic_method_call only does `checked.push(self.pass_receiver_to(receiver, receiver_mode, def, receiver_span))`. With receiver.ty = Derived, receiver_by_address(Derived, def) is true (the result is a view), so borrow_argument produces `ExprKind::Ref` of type `ref Derived`, and no cast is ever inserted. The instance's first parameter is still `ref Base`. MIR does not check argument types, and the C backend renders Direct call arguments verbatim (call_expression 7166-7191). The C therefore passes a `struct em_obj_Derived**` to a `struct em_obj_Base**` parameter. GCC 14+ rejects this by default (-Wincompatible-pointer-types); clang and MSVC (/W3, C4133) warn. Both break [CG-C-2]. The callee then reads a `struct Derived*` through a `struct Base*` lvalue, the exact undefined behaviour ADR-134 set out to remove ([CG-C-1]). Before D-460 this call was correctly typed: a retained upcast temporary was borrowed as `ref Base`. The `mut self` generic case has the same gap, but that one predates D-460: the Mode::Mut cast at 38291 is also after the generic return.

findings.title: D-460 covers only a plain local: an inherited view getter called on `self` (or through a `ref Derived` local) inside a derived method still borrows a released temporary (E3060)
findings.evidence: The new path requires `matches!(receiver.kind, ExprKind::Local(_))`. A by-address `self` (a borrowed receiver of a method whose result is a view, [BRW-8]) is a local of type `ref Derived`, and read_local_expecting returns it as `ExprKind::Deref(Box::new(read))`, so it is not ExprKind::Local. The same holds for a `ref Derived` local or a `mut d: Derived` parameter. For these receivers the old branch runs: `receiver = self.coerce(receiver, receiver_ty)` (a ClassUpcast cast expression), then pass_receiver_to/borrow_argument wraps it in `ExprKind::Ref { place: <cast> }`. That materialises a temporary handle released at the statement's end, which is exactly D-460's symptom. By [LT-1] rule 1 the result borrows the receiver, and `self` is the caller's handle, not a handle stored in an object ([RC-5]'s retained-copy case). So keeping the view past the statement, or returning it, should be accepted, as it is for a call on `self` in Base itself. I could not run the compiler to confirm the E3060, and no conformance test covers this shape, hence low confidence.

results.summary: I reviewed outer_loop and lift in compiler/ember_analysis/src/loop_access.rs, plus the code they depend on: the inner hoisting (candidate, mut_self_call_on_root, apply), range_facts' reverse_postorder, loop_headers and natural_loops, loop_version::retarget, check_hoisting::runs_no_ember_code, and the pass order in ember_driver main.rs. I also read how the C backend emits BeginAccess and EndAccess, the back-to-back check form, the field and object checks, Assign (retain, never release) and println, and its for-loop and scoped-local detection. On the spec side I read ADR-158, [EXC-1..19], [PAN-1] and ODR-072/E2103. I could not build a single Ember program where the longer hold changes behaviour or safety, so I report no findings. The reason is that the extended hold is invisible unless something checks or changes the access words, and the outer-loop filter shuts out every way that could happen. Every per-field and whole-object check is a BeginAccess statement (including the back-to-back check form and Shared accesses), and those are refused outside the bracket. Ember code is refused because only built-in calls on the runs_no_ember_code list are allowed. Drops are refused. Panics abort. Writes to projected places are refused. The receiver local is never named except by the `t = &mut root` setup, and t is used only by the bracket's direct mut-self call. Lowering emits that call's BeginAccess only for a `self` receiver, and E2103 stops a method from re-pointing self, so the receiver names one object for the whole hold. Because the access state of the object's words cannot change between turns, one check at the first begin fails exactly when the per-turn checks would have. The CFG rewrite is also equivalent: every edge out of the single exit in the copy goes through end_block. Return and Unreachable blocks fall outside a natural loop, so their edges count as exits. A zero-trip inner loop simply runs on unchanged. The three-deep case lifts correctly a second time from the original preheader through the first lift's copies. The one leftover is cosmetic: the original post-begin blocks of a lifted loop stay in the body unreachable, which costs only some later pattern matching (for example for-loop recognition and quiet-call predecessor counts), not correctness.
checked_ok: Field-setup (ODR-065 kept-copy) inner hoists can never be lifted: their prelude in the original body block (`copy = root.f` or `t = &mut root.f`) names the receiver outside the bracket, and sets_up only accepts an unprojected `&mut root`, so only the [EXC-15] mut-self form lifts

Receiver identity is stable for the hold. The receiver is never assigned or named outside the bracket except by `t = &mut root`. Every `&mut root` local is unusable in any statement and, inside the loop, only as an argument of the bracket's Direct call. That call is a mut-self method, since lowering emits BeginAccess only when the receiver is `self`, and E2103 (typeck lib.rs ~19997 and ~35757) forbids assigning self or passing it to re-point a handle

No check can see the longer hold. Per-field checks, whole-object checks, back-to-back check forms (codegen emit_block_stmts) and HEAP-5 Shared accesses are all BeginAccess/EndAccess statements, refused outside the bracket. Copy-field reads and writes are never checked ([EXC-17])

Nothing else runs Ember code under the hold. Only the runs_no_ember_code built-ins are allowed. println of a class prints class and address in C, and of a struct prints field-wise Debug, so no user code runs. ArrayClear and ArrayTruncate are limited to scalar elements. Drop statements are refused, and codegen's Assign retains but never releases, so no implicit drop runs
Panic paths are safe: Assert failures abort ([PAN-1]) with no unwinding, defers or destructors, and an f-string message is formatted before the Assert through calls the filter refuses

Single exit: natural_loops builds blocks backwards from the latches using reachable predecessors only, so a block ending in Return or Unreachable is outside the loop and the edge into it counts as an exit. A loop with an early return to a different block, or none at all, is refused. When all exits share one target, every edge to it in the copy goes through end_block via held()

lift's copy matches the original. The begin is removed only from the copy of the preheader and the matching end only from the copy of the postheader. retarget covers Goto, SwitchInt, Call and Assert. Edges inside the loop go to copies, the exit goes to end_block, and the original preheader then continues in the copy, which leaves the original post-begin blocks unreachable

An inner loop that does not run is handled: before the first begin the original runs as written and checks nothing; after it, turns whose inner loop does not run simply keep the hold, and no code that could observe it runs

Three-deep nests work. After the first lift the copy region is entered only at call_block', so the CFG stays reducible. The second lift's bracket (the original begin_block, the copies, and end_block) sits inside the next loop's natural loop. Its own begin stays at preheader_statement 0, the copied begin_block' has none, and end_block's end is removed from the second copy. The while-let terminates because the copied headers fall inside the bracket

A sibling hoisted access in the same outer loop, on the same receiver or another, blocks the lift because its BeginAccess is outside the first bracket. check_hoisting records are not present yet: that pass runs at main.rs:3133, after this one

The order of later passes fits: convert_quiet_calls only touches a begin that sits in a call block, so it skips the lifted begin; remove_never_firing_checks runs after the hold is final. The C for-loop detector requires one predecessor per chain block, so jumping into a copy cannot produce a missing label. loop_scoped_locals declares a local inside each loop only when every use is in that loop

Generators: a yield inside the outer loop is either a second exit (refused) or the only exit, and then end_block ends the hold before the suspension. Frame-field receivers are projected and never become candidates

results.summary: I found no real defect in the D-201 String vs Array[u8] split. I read the type table (`ember_types/src/lib.rs` near 189, 1007 and 3096), and `ember_typeck/src/lib.rs` near 7205 plus the other text/non-text sites, namely slicing, indexing, `for` loops, `in`, method dispatch, coercion and view creation, equality, hashing, printing and the `to_str` conversion. I also read the codegen sites that key on the text flag (Slice, StringAsStr, display, comptime dump, ordering) and `const_eval.rs`. The split holds at every site I read. Text paths test `is_text` or `text: true`, and collection paths take only `text: false`. A `String` unifies with no `Array[T]` and matches no `extend[T] Array[T]`. `Array[u8]` slices to `Span[u8]` and prints as numbers. The only route from bytes to text I found is `Span[u8].to_str()`, which runs `Utf8Valid` first, and `ember_utf8_valid` in the runtime is correct. Nothing I read indexes or mutates a `String` as bytes. I read everything and ran nothing, per the rules. The lower-level uses of `Vec { elem, .. }` (analysis passes, drop glue, C helpers, and the `Vec { .. }` arms in typeck that I did not trace) were read only by grep, not traced. They cover representation, not text semantics, so I did not follow them further.
checked_ok: Type table: `String` is `Vec{u8, text:true}` and `Array[u8]` is `Vec{u8, text:false}`, so they are different interned types. `unify_with_fixed` (types lib 1007) and `match_generic_extension_type` (typeck 7205) require equal text flags. `builtin_generic_origin` and `instance_stem` map only `text:false` to "Array", so `extend[T] Array[T]` and Array-typed generic parameters do not match a String.

Slicing (`synth_slice`, typeck 23790-23850): String and str give a `Slice{text:true}` over `str` with a character-boundary check in MIR (`lower_slice` -> `StrIsCharBoundary`). `Array[u8]` gives a `Slice{text:false}` over `Span[u8]`. Codegen `view_parts` and the Slice rvalue both key on `text`.

Indexing (typeck 30443-30530) accepts `Vec{text:false}` only, so `s[i]` and `s[i] = x` on a String give "cannot index". `builtin_index_method_fits`, the `Index` std impl and `Span` coercion (29408) also require `text:false`, so a String is not passed as `Span[u8]` or `MutSpan[u8]`.

Method dispatch: `push`, `pop`, `insert`, `remove`, `truncate`, `reserve`, `clear` and `capacity` on a String go through `synth_string_mutation`, `StringPushChar` or `StringPush`. The Array-only methods (`sort`, `extend`, `drain`, `swap`, `get_mut`, `as_span`, `as_mut_span`, `iter`, `chunks`, `windows`, `split_at`) are gated by `text:false` or `!is_string`. `as_str` is String-only. `String += str` goes through `StringPush`.

Printing and format: `is_display_aggregate` is `!text`. `debug_stmt` tests `text_pair` first, so a String prints quoted text and `Array[u8]` goes through the generated `fmt_fn` as `[104, 105]`. `format_suffix` tests `text:true`. The format-spec check (`is_text`) and the comptime dump (`s<len>:<hex>` vs `v<len>`) also key on the flag.

Bytes to text: `Span[u8].to_str()` (typeck 44947-45000) is the only conversion I found. It runs `Builtin::Utf8Valid` and returns `Result[str, Utf8Error]`. `ember_utf8_valid` (ember_rt.c 3125) rejects overlongs (C0/C1, E0, F0), surrogates (ED), values above U+10FFFF (F4, F5+), truncated sequences and stray continuation bytes. `const_eval` rebuilds a constant String with `String::from_utf8(...).ok()?`.

Equality, hashing and order: `has_implicit_eq`, `hashes` and `synth_eq_of` treat both as byte or element sequences, which is the same memcmp. std has separate `Hash` impls (`extend String` hashes the bytes plus 255, and `extend[T] Array[T]` hashes the length plus elements). `sortable` and `totally_ordered` reject `Array`, so the codegen `unreachable!` in `less_behind_pointers` for `text:false` is not reachable from a checked program.

Loops and membership: `for` over a String uses `check_for_text`, and over `Array[u8]` uses `check_for_array` (`text:false`). `x in s` on text uses `StrContains` or `StrContainsChar`, and on `Array[u8]` uses the element scan. `len(s)` on a String is rejected with E2073.

Open-local inference (`fix_open_local`, 23733): `Vec{..} => ty` can fix an empty `[]` local as `String` when it is passed where a String is expected. The re-check of `[]` against `String` then reports E2060 (`vec_elem` requires `text:false`), so no invalid program is accepted. At worst the error message is confusing.

results.summary: Read-only review of the D-355 (zero-sized unit in buffers/boxes) and D-358 (out-of-line drop glue for nested containers) code in compiler/ember_codegen_c/src/lib.rs, plus the runtime's zero-size handling (ember_rt.c). The core of both fixes looks correct. c_size/c_align/element_pointer/buffer_element/value_address are applied consistently in Array helpers (pop, remove, swap_remove, drain, truncate, extend, clear, clone, sorted), push/insert/reverse/swap/reserve, box and shared construction, drop of Vec and Box, spans (SpanIterNext, chunks, split), alloc/free builtins and size_of. The runtime never returns NULL for size 0 (raw_alloc and the arena and fixed-arena paths bump 0 to 1, and ct_alloc does too), so `*(char*)ptr` on a non-empty Array[()] is safe. Void struct, tuple, enum and fixed-array members are all a uint8_t byte via c_member_type, so Option[()], tuples containing () and MapSlot[K, ()] are well-formed C. Debug, equality and sort of void elements ignore the element text. Drop glue (drop_glue_call/drop_nests/owns_itself) gives at most one loop, switch or deref per C function. Spurious `true` from the `seen` set only adds an unneeded glue function; it never drops less. I found two gaps: arena allocation of a () value, and Debug printing through deeply nested Box/Cell/Ref, which still nests one C level per type level. Both are medium to low confidence, and I could not run any program.
checked_ok: c_size/c_align/element_pointer/buffer_element/value_address and the Array helper bodies (pop, remove, swap_remove, drain, truncate, extend, clear, clone, sorted) for void elements

Runtime zero-size handling: vec_reserve, vec_from_elems, vec_insert, swap, reverse, box_new_copy, arena_alloc_*, fixed_arena_alloc_copy, ember_ct_alloc all give a non-NULL pointer and a consistent alloc/free size for size 0
Box[()] construction (value_address, box_new_copy(0,1,&(uint8_t){0})) and drop (free with c_size 0 / align 1)
Option[()], tuples with (), enum payloads and MapSlot[K, ()] fields use c_member_type (uint8_t); Option niche rules never select a void payload
Debug printing of Array[()], Span[()], Map[K, ()] and Set: debug_stmt returns '()' before touching the element expression; the `(void const*)v->ptr)[i]` text is never emitted
eq_expr/emit_eq_fns: one function per aggregate type, passed by pointer, so no C nesting grows with type depth; void is `1`

drop_glue_call/drop_nests/owns_itself: every Vec element, Box payload and enum payload that opens a loop/switch/deref goes out of line, so each glue function is one level deep; struct/tuple/fixed-array fields inline only sequential statements
clone_parts helpers are per-type functions taking pointers; Array clone/extend for void skips per-element work
comptime_dump of Vec[()]/tuples/structs with void parts ignores the element access text

findings.title: Arena alloc of a () value emits `&0`, which is not valid C
findings.evidence: Builtin::ArenaAlloc, FixedArenaAlloc and ScopedArenaAlloc build `arena_alloc_copy(state, {c_size}, {c_align}, &{})` with `&{}` filled by `rendered[1]` directly. A void operand renders as "0" (`Const::Void => "0"` at line 8850; `Operand::Copy/Move` of a void place => "0" at line 8802), giving `&0`, an invalid lvalue. Box::new, Shared::new and Array insert/push use `self.value_address(&rendered[..], elem)` (line 9479), which produces `&(uint8_t){0}` for void, but these three arena builtins do not use it. The runtime already copes with a 1-byte read (arena_alloc_copy uses copy_size 1 when size is 0).

findings.title: Debug printing through nested Box/Cell/Ref still nests parentheses per type level
findings.evidence: debug_stmt handles a compiler Box, a Cell and a Ref inline and recursively: `printed_payload` returns `(*({v}))` or `(({v}).value)`, then `return self.debug_stmt(out, &payload, inner)`; the `TyKind::Ref` arm does the same with `(*({v}))`. Each level adds two parentheses to the expression and no fmt function is requested for the intermediate type, unlike Array/tuple/struct/enum, which each get their own fmt function (D-358-style one-level nesting). A type nested to the [GRM-39] limit of 256 levels (e.g. Box[Box[...Box[i32]...]]) therefore produces a C expression with about 512 nested parentheses, past clang's default -fbracket-depth of 256 (error: parentheses nested too deeply). That limit is reached at roughly 128 levels. Drop (drop_nests), equality and Array/struct/tuple/enum printing are fine; this printing path is the one helper I found that still nests per level.

findings.title: Retain lines for Copy types holding class handles nest a switch per enum level
findings.evidence: retain_lines_for_value recurses inline for Enum payloads, emitting `switch (tag) { case N: { <nested switch...> } break; ... }` once per enum level, and Array arm unrolls `0..len` statements. No out-of-line retain glue exists, unlike drop glue (D-358). A Copy value of Option[Option[...[Class]...]] nested ~85+ levels deep (3 brace levels per level) would exceed clang's 256 limit. Also reached from clone_part_lines and the Array Clone/Extend helpers. It is rare because it needs a Copy aggregate of nested payload enums over class handles.
findings.program:
class C:
    x: i32
enum W:
    One(Option[Option[ ... (200 deep) ... Option[C]]])
fn f(w: W) -> W:
    return w   # Copy of a value holding a class handle emits the nested retain switches
# C compiler reports bracket nesting too deep. Low confidence: depends on Option[Option[...]] being Copy-with-handle at that depth and on the retain path being taken.
